sections.heading: Why bitcoin miners became AI's landlords
bullets: Bitcoin mining and AI compute want the same scarce input — hundreds of megawatts of cheap, grid-connected power — but AI pays roughly 10x more per megawatt-hour of use

Miners spent 2018-2024 assembling exactly what AI now queues years for: energized substations, transmission rights, and industrially-zoned land in cheap-power regions (West Texas ERCOT, British Columbia hydro)
The conversion is a rebuild, not a rebrand: mining halls run ~$1M/MW of cheap air-cooled shelving with no redundancy; AI hosting needs $10M+/MW of liquid cooling, UPS, and concurrent maintainability
Conversion has an accounting signature: the miner voluntarily impairs (writes off) working ASICs to free the megawatts — a company destroying its own P&L on purpose to redeploy its power

sections.heading: The vertical-integration spectrum
bullets: Three neocloud business models sit on one spectrum: pure landlords lease shells at ~$1.4M/MW-year (lowest tech risk), bare-metal GPU clouds rent hardware at mid-single-digit $M/MW-year, and full-stack platforms with software and services capture $10-15M/MW-year (highest refresh risk)
Owning your power AND running the cloud captures both margins but demands both skill sets: utility-scale construction and hyperscaler-grade software operations — very different muscles
Vertical integration shows up in the gross margin and in schedule control: no colocation landlord to wait on, no ground-lease escalators — but also no one else to blame for delays
The software layer is the hardest part to build and the easiest to buy: acquiring an enterprise cloud-software company grafts twenty years of orchestration maturity onto a three-year-old cloud

sections.heading: Reading a transition-period income statement
bullets: When a company dismantles one business while building another, quarterly revenue can FALL while the enterprise grows: the dying segment shrinks on schedule, the growing one recognizes revenue only when capacity commissions
Consensus estimates break down structurally: analysts can't model the timing of decommissioning against commissioning, so 30%+ 'misses' coexist with record contract signings
Non-cash noise dominates: hardware impairments, unrealized gains/losses on capped calls and prepaid forwards, and stock-comp swings can move a quarter by hundreds of millions with zero cash effect
The metrics that track reality: contracted ARR (annualized run-rate under signed contracts), MW commissioned vs plan, and prepayment percentages — prepaid contracts are demand you can bank

sections.heading: GPU financing: from converts to investment grade
bullets: Convertible notes fund the land-grab phase: near-zero coupons in exchange for future dilution, stacked in successive tranches with 'capped calls' bought alongside to limit the dilution up to a share-price cap
Each convert announcement is a market event — investors punish supply overhang even when the capital is contractually required by signed customer deals

Graduation is an investment-grade rating on GPU-backed debt: a rated facility (private placement + delayed-draw term loan) against a hyperscaler contract can fund ~96% of the GPU capex at low-single-digit all-in cost once prepayments count
Customer prepayments are the cheapest capital of all: 20-45% cash up front converts the customer into the project's co-financier and collapses payback periods

sections.heading: When the chip vendor is customer, partner, and shareholder
bullets: The strongest possible endorsement stack: the GPU maker certifies your cloud (reference architectures, exemplar programs), buys your services for its own R&D, and takes a right to buy your equity
The same stack is the circularity critique: vendor-financed and vendor-purchased demand can overstate organic demand, and partnership announcements ('up to 5 GW') carry no guaranteed chip allocations
How to tell the difference: watch for third-party customers signing at higher $/MW than the anchor deals, and for delivered-and-accepted milestones rather than announced intentions

Independent quality ratings vs vendor certifications can directly conflict — one measures operations maturity across dozens of criteria, the other measures conformance to the vendor's architecture. Both can be true at once

sections.heading: Multi-grid strategy: why geography is risk management
bullets: Single-grid concentration (e.g., all-ERCOT) means one regulator, one price regime, one congestion pattern — diversifying into a second grid (SPP/Oklahoma) and other countries hedges the whole platform

Renewable-heavy grids (Texas wind, BC hydro, South Australia's near-100% renewable target) offer both cheap energy and location-based clean-power claims — but without PPAs or RECs, 'renewable-powered' is grid-mix arithmetic, not contracted supply
Southern-hemisphere and European sites add sovereign-AI demand and submarine-fiber adjacency to Asia — geography as a sales strategy, not just a cost strategy

An energized-but-untenanted gigawatt is both the biggest asset and the biggest question mark: live grid capacity with no signed customer is pure optionality, valuable exactly until the market decides it's overbuild

flashcards.q: Why is a bitcoin-mining site a head start for AI infrastructure?
flashcards.a: It already owns the scarce inputs — energized substations, transmission rights, and cheap-power land — that AI projects queue years for. The buildings and cooling get replaced; the grid connection is the inheritance.

flashcards.q: What does it mean when a miner impairs working ASICs?
flashcards.a: A voluntary write-off of functioning mining hardware to free its megawatts for GPUs — deliberately damaging the current P&L to redeploy power into a higher-value use. It's the clearest accounting signature of a real pivot.

flashcards.q: Rank the three neocloud business models by revenue per MW and by risk.
flashcards.a: Landlords ~$1.4M/MW-yr (lowest tech risk), bare-metal GPU clouds mid-single-digit $M/MW-yr, full-stack platforms $10-15M/MW-yr (highest hardware-refresh and software risk). More stack = more margin = more ways to fail.

flashcards.q: Why can revenue fall while a transition company is actually growing?
flashcards.a: The dying segment (mining) shrinks immediately when hardware is decommissioned; the growing segment (cloud) recognizes revenue only when capacity commissions. The gap between those schedules is a revenue air pocket.

flashcards.q: Name three non-cash items that can swing a quarter by hundreds of millions.
flashcards.a: Hardware impairments, unrealized gains/losses on derivatives like capped calls and prepaid forwards, and stock-compensation charges. None touch cash; all wreck EPS comparability.

flashcards.q: What is contracted ARR and why prefer it to reported revenue during a buildout?
flashcards.a: Annualized run-rate revenue under signed contracts (GPU-hour price × 8,760 hours + ancillaries). It measures the business being built; reported revenue measures the one being dismantled.

flashcards.q: What is a capped call and why buy one alongside a convertible note?
flashcards.a: A derivative that offsets the note's dilution if shares convert, up to a set price cap. The issuer pays cash now to cap future share issuance — softening the dilution objection to each raise.

flashcards.q: What does an investment-grade rating on a GPU financing signal?
flashcards.a: That rating agencies treat the underlying customer contract and hardware as bankable collateral. It cuts funding cost dramatically — and combined with customer prepayments can cover nearly all the GPU capex.

flashcards.q: Why are customer prepayments the best capital in this sector?
flashcards.a: A 20-45% cash advance makes the customer co-finance its own capacity: no coupon, no dilution, shortened payback, and it proves the demand is real enough that the buyer commits cash before delivery.

flashcards.q: How do you distinguish real demand from vendor circularity?
flashcards.a: Look for third-party customers paying equal-or-higher $/MW than the vendor-linked anchor deals, and for delivered-and-accepted milestones. Vendor partnerships 'up to X GW' with no guaranteed allocations are intentions, not demand.

flashcards.q: Can a cloud be 'Underperforming' to one rater and 'Exemplar' to the chip vendor at once?
flashcards.a: Yes — independent ratings score operational/software maturity across many criteria; vendor certifications verify conformance to the vendor's reference architecture and performance targets. They measure different things.

flashcards.q: Why diversify across power grids and countries?
flashcards.a: One grid means one regulator, one price regime, one congestion/curtailment pattern. A second grid (or continent) hedges regulatory and price risk, and international sites unlock sovereign-AI demand the home market can't.
